A thermometer is placed into a water bath and displays a reading of 50∘C. The thermometer is then transferred to a 10∘C water bath, and its reading begins to decrease. After 5 minutes, the thermometer reading is 40∘C. To the nearest minute, how long does it take for the thermometer to register a reading of 30∘C?

Hint: You may assume that the temperature reading T(t) of the thermometer decreases at a rate that obeys Newton's law of cooling, where T is measured in degrees Celsius and t>0 is the time, in minutes, since the thermometer was transferred into the 10∘C water bath.

Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature T(t) of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the inhibited decay equation

dTdt=−k(T−TS),

where TS is the temperature of the surroundings, and k>0 is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, TS=10∘C, and we have

dTdt=−k(T−10).

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

dTT−10=−kdt∫dTT−10=−k∫dtln⁡|T−10|=−kt+C

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have T−10>0 for all t>0. Next, we solve for T(t), as follows:

T−10=e−kt+CT−10=eCe−ktT−10=Ke−ktT=10+Ke−kt

Note that K=eC is a constant of integration.

We're told that the initial temperature reading was 50∘C. So, we apply the initial condition T(0)=50, and solve for K:

50=10+Ke050=10+KK=40

Therefore, we have the following expression for T(t):

T(t)=10+40e−kt

We're also told that, after 5 minutes, the thermometer reading is 40∘C. So, applying the condition T(5)=40, we can solve for k:

40=10+40e−5k30=40e−5k34=e−5kln⁡(34)=−5kk=−15ln⁡(34)

Finally, let t1 be the time when the thermometer reads 30∘C. Then, we have

T(t1)=3010+40e−kt1=3040e−kt1=20e−kt1=12−kt1=ln⁡(12)t1=−1kln⁡(12).

Substituting in our value for k, we conclude that the thermometer will read 30∘C after

t1=−ln⁡(12)−15ln⁡(34)≈12min,

rounded to the nearest minute.

html: The number of particles N(t) in a radioactive substance after t years can be modeled by the differential equation dNdt=−3N. If there were 8500 particles initially, calculate the number of particles remaining after 2 years. Round your answer to the nearest integer.

We model the number of particles in the substance using the differential equation dNdt=−3N.

The solution to this equation is N(t)=N0e−3t, where N0 is the initial value.

We're told that there were 8500 particles initially, so we have N0=8500.

Therefore, the number of particles N at time t is N(t)=8500e−3t.

Finally, to find the number of particles when t=2, we substitute t=2 into the above, as follows: N(2)=8500e−3⋅2=8500e−6≈21.069

Rounding our answer to the nearest integer, we conclude that 21 particles remain.

We model the amount of debt remaining using the differential equation dLdt=−0.5L.

The solution to this equation is L(t)=L0e−0.5t, where L0 is the initial value.

A first-order ordinary differential equation that is written in the form dydx=f(x,y) is said to be homogeneous if it satisfies the following property: f(tx,ty)=f(x,y)

The only option in which this is the case is dydx=2xyx2+y2.

We can check this using one of two methods.

Method 1

Let f(x,y)=2xyx2+y2.

We see that both the numerator and denominator are homogeneous polynomials of degree 2. Therefore, f(x,y) is a homogeneous function of degree 2−2=0.

Hence, the original differential equation is homogeneous.

Method 2

To check this in detail using the definition, we first write: f(x,y)=2xyx2+y2

We can check that this is homogeneous showing that f(tx,ty)=f(x,y), as follows:

f(tx,ty)=2(tx)(ty)(tx)2+(ty)2=t2⋅2xyt2x2+t2y2= t2⋅2xyt2(x2+y2)=2xyx2+y2=f(x,y)

Since f(tx,ty)=f(x,y), the original differential equation is homogeneous.

Your Answer:

A University Campus has a total of 1500 students. At the beginning of the new semester at the University, flu affected 300 students. After 10 days, the number of students affected by the flu increases to 500. To the nearest day, how long does it take for the flu-stricken campus population to reach 800 students?

Hint: You may assume that the number of students affected by the flu, P(t), increases at a rate that obeys an inhibited growth model, where t≥0 is the time, in days.

The rate at which the campus population affected by the flu, P(t), changes is proportional to the difference between the total campus population and its current population affected. Therefore, we have the inhibited growth equation dPdt=k(a−P), where a is the total population of the campus, and k>0 is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, a=1500 students, and we have

dPdt=k(1500−P).

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

dP1500−P=kdt∫dP1500−P=∫kdt−ln⁡|1500−P|=kt+C

Since this is the solution to an inhibited growth equation, we have 1500−P>0 for all t≥0. Next, we solve for P(t), as follows: 1500−P=e−kt−C1500−P=e−Ce−kt1500−P=Ke−ktP=1500−Ke−kt

Note that K=e−C is a constant of integration.

We're told that the initial campus population affected by the flu was 300 students. So, we apply the initial condition P(0)=300, and solve for K: P(0)=3001500−Ke0=3001500−K=300K=1200

Therefore, we have the following expression for P(t):

P(t)=1500−1200e−kt

We're also told that, after 10 days, the campus population affected by flu was 500 students. So, applying the condition P(10)=500, we can solve for k: P(10)=5001500−1200e−10k=5001000=1200e−10ke−10k=56−10k=ln⁡(56)k=−110ln⁡(56)

Finally, let t1 be the time when 800 students are affected by the flu. Then, we have P(t1)=8001500−1200e−kt1=800700=1200e−kt1e−kt1=712−kt1=ln⁡(712)t1=−1kln⁡(712).

Substituting in our value for k, we conclude that 800 students will be affected by the flu after t1=−ln⁡(712)−110ln⁡(56)=29.562…≈30days, rounded to the nearest day.

Suppose the functions y1(x) and y2(x) are defined on some interval I. The Wronskian W(y1,y2) of these functions is defined as W(y1,y2)=|y1y2y1′y2′|=y1y2′−y2y1′.

Recall the following:

  • If W≠0 for at least one x∈I, then y1 and y2 are linearly independent.

  • If W=0 and it’s known that y1 and y2 are solutions to the same second-order linear differential equation, then y1 and y2 are linearly dependent.

In our case, the Wronskian is given by

W(y1,y2)=|e2x+1e2x(e2x+1)′(e2x)′|=|e2x+1e2x2e2x+12e2x|=e2x+1⋅2e2x−e2x⋅2e2x+1=2e4x+1−2e4x+1=0

which is zero for all x∈R.

Therefore, the set {y1(x),y2(x)} is linearly dependent on R.

Which of the following is a first-order homogeneous ordinary differential equation?

A first-order ordinary differential equation that is written in the form dydx=f(x,y) is said to be homogeneous if it satisfies the following property: f(tx,ty)=f(x,y)

The only option in which this is the case is dydx=x3−3x2y+xy2y3+x3.

We can check this using one of two methods.

Method 1

Let f(x,y)=x3−3x2y+xy2y3+x3.

We see that both the numerator and denominator are homogeneous polynomials of degree 3. Therefore, f(x,y) is a homogeneous function of degree 3−3=0.

Hence, the original differential equation is homogeneous.

Method 2

To check this in detail using the definition, we first write: f(x,y)=x3−3x2y+xy2y3+x3

We can check that this is homogeneous showing that f(tx,ty)=f(x,y), as follows:

f(tx,ty)=(tx)3−3(tx)2(ty)+(tx)(ty)2(ty)3+(tx)3=t3(x3)−t3(3x2y)+t3(xy2)t3y3+t3x3=t3(x3−3x2y+xy2)t3(y3+x3)=x3−3x2y+xy2y3+x3=f(x,y)

Since f(tx,ty)=f(x,y), the original differential equation is homogeneous.

where a is the maximum capacity of the data center, and k>0 is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, a=1000 computers, and we have

T−25=e−kt+CT−25=eCe−ktT−25=Ke−ktT=25+Ke−kt

Note that K=eC is a constant of integration.

100=25+Ke0100=25+KK=75

Therefore, we have the following expression for T(t):

T(t)=25+75e−kt

Substituting in our value for k, we conclude that the temperature of water will be 30∘C after

The only option in which this is the case is dydx=y2−x2x2+y2.

Hence, the original differential equation is homogeneous.
